chapter.name: The Constitution of India: An Introduction

questions.q: True or False: In the chapter's kabaddi story, the dispute was settled by the referee alone; the captains had no say, and the rulebook only helped her to decide. Give a reason for your verdict.
questions.a: False. The team captains conferred with the referee and looked at the rules together, and they then agreed that the player was out. The dispute ended amicably because all concerned accepted the same rulebook.
s: Verdict: False
Reason: the captains conferred with the referee, looked at the rules and agreed

questions.q: Dr. Rajendra Prasad said a democratic Constitution works only if those who work with it have 'willingness to respect the viewpoint of others, capacity for compromise and accommodation'. (i) Which two moments in the kabaddi story show this willingness? (ii) Why would a rulebook that one captain refused to look at fail to settle the dispute?
questions.a: (i) The captains conferred with the referee, and after looking at the rules they agreed that the player was out. (ii) A rulebook settles a dispute only when all concerned accept it; if one captain would not refer to it, there would be no common text to end the argument.
s: Captains confer with the referee
They look at the rules and agree on the result
A rulebook works only if all agree to refer to it

questions.q: A museum curator must store a century-old handwritten register. She wants a gas for the display case and uses the same reason the chapter gives for the helium case that holds the Constitution. Which property should she look for?
questions.a: The chapter says helium is a gas that does not react with paper or ink, which helps preserve the Constitution over time. The curator needs the same property for her handwritten register.
o: That it does not react with paper or ink
That it is lighter than air, so pages do not press on the glass
That it keeps out insects and moulds from the shelf
That it soaks up moisture from the pages

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A document that only lists the punishments for people who break laws would fall short of being a constitution.
Reason (R): A constitution also frames the three organs of government, sets checks and balances, states the rights and duties of citizens and outlines the nation's long-term goals.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both statements are true. The chapter lists what a constitution lays out, and a list of punishments covers none of these four things, so R explains A.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: The chapter says the Constitution is 'something like' a rulebook. Give one way in which the Constitution goes beyond the kabaddi rulebook and support it with an example from the chapter.
questions.a: Any one: the Constitution states values and ideals (equality and justice for all, fraternity, pluralism, freedom) that form the basis of laws; or it lays out the rights and duties of citizens; or it frames the three organs and their checks and balances. The kabaddi rulebook only settles disputes in a match.
s: A valid way the Constitution goes beyond a game rulebook
A supporting example drawn from the chapter

questions.q: Aarav says, 'A constitution is a rulebook for the people in government. It tells the legislature, the executive and the judiciary what to do, but it says nothing about ordinary citizens or the country's aims.' How far is he right? Answer with the chapter.
questions.a: Partly right. He is right that a constitution frames the three organs and their roles and responsibilities. He is wrong to say it is silent on citizens and aims: it also lays out the rights and duties of citizens and outlines the long-term goals and aspirations of the nation.
s: Verdict: partly right
The right half: it frames the organs and their roles
The wrong half: it also lays out rights, duties and long-term goals

questions.q: Ritu's quiz card asks: 'The Constitution now has 25 parts and 12 schedules. By how many has the combined number of parts and schedules grown since it came into effect?' Which answer is correct?
questions.a: When it came into effect it had 22 parts and 8 schedules, a total of 30; today the total is 25 + 12 = 37. The growth is 7 (3 parts and 4 schedules).

questions.q: At a swearing-in, a High Court judge reads aloud that she 'promises to follow the provisions of the Constitution'. Her friend says, 'That is the same oath the President takes.' Which reply agrees with the chapter?
questions.a: The chapter says the President takes an oath to preserve, protect and defend the Constitution, while the prime minister, the council of ministers and judges promise to follow its provisions. So the pledges are worded differently, though all uphold the Constitution.
o: Not the same: the President's oath is to preserve, protect and defend it, while judges promise to follow its provisions
The same: all high officials take one common oath to preserve, protect and defend the Constitution of the country
Not the same: judges alone pledge to the Constitution, while the President pledges only to Parliament and its members
The same: the President and judges both promise to follow its provisions, and only the prime minister swears to defend it

questions.q: Compare the kabaddi rulebook with the Constitution of India. Give two similarities and two differences, using what the chapter says a constitution lays out.
questions.a: Similarities: both are written texts that are consulted when a dispute arises; both work because the people concerned agree to follow them (captains and referee; officials who pledge to uphold the Constitution). Differences: the Constitution frames the three organs and checks and balances, which a game rulebook does not; it lays out the rights and duties of citizens; it states values and goals for a whole nation, where the rulebook only governs one sport.
s: Two similarities
Two differences using the four contents
A concluding sentence on why the Constitution is 'something like' a rulebook

questions.q: A district court cancels an order of the collector's office because the order goes against the Constitution. (a) Which two organs of government are involved here? (b) Which feature of the Constitution does this show at work?
questions.a: (a) The executive (the collector's office, which implements) and the judiciary (the court, which ensures actions and laws accord with the Constitution). (b) Checks and balances among the organs, which ensure fairness, responsibility and accountability.
s: Part (a): executive and judiciary identified with their roles
Part (b): checks and balances ensuring accountability

questions.q: A new country's constitution has one sentence: 'The Prime Minister shall govern for the good of all.' (a) Which organ of government does the sentence mention, and which two organs does it leave out? (b) Which feature of a constitution would be missing, so that nobody could question the Prime Minister's decisions?
questions.a: (a) It mentions the executive (headed by the prime minister) and leaves out the legislature and the judiciary. (b) Checks and balances among the organs, which ensure fairness, responsibility and accountability.
s: Part (a): executive mentioned; legislature and judiciary left out
Part (b): checks and balances, giving accountability

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The Indian Constitution is the world's largest written constitution.
Reason (R): The Constitution has stayed unchanged at 22 parts and 8 schedules since it came into effect.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: A is true as the chapter states. R is false: it came into effect with 22 parts and 8 schedules and now has 25 parts and 12 schedules.
o: A is true, but R is false.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: The Haveri District Cricket Association's rulebook gives a Selection Committee the power to pick teams, a Match Committee the power to run tournaments and a Disciplinary Committee the power to decide complaints. It lists each player's rights and duties and states a goal of 'a first-class player from every taluka in twelve years'. It says nothing about how one committee may question another. Which of the four things a constitution lays out is this rulebook missing?
questions.a: The framework of the organs (three bodies with roles), the rights and duties, and the long-term goal are all present. What is absent is any way for one body to be held answerable to another, which is checks and balances.
o: Checks and balances among the committees
The framework and roles of the committees
The rights and duties of the players
The long-term goals of the association

questions.q: In a mind-map of what a constitution contains, a student writes 'equality and justice for all' under 'political system'. Correct her: in which box does the chapter place such ideals, and what relationship does it say they have with the laws and principles of a constitution?
questions.a: They belong under the values and ideals of a society. The chapter says it is these values and ideals that usually form the basis for the laws and principles in a constitution.
s: Placed under values and ideals of a society
Values and ideals form the basis for the laws and principles

questions.q: The Student Club's Planning Team frames its rules and a Disputes Panel decides whether a rule was broken. The third body its constitution still needs, to carry the rules out, matches the ___ organ of government.
questions.a: executive

questions.q:
Read the statements about what a constitution lays out.
1. Checks and balances among the organs of government are meant to ensure fairness, responsibility and accountability.
2. A constitution's values and ideals are separate from its laws; the laws are drawn up without reference to those values.
3. The Indian Constitution lays out the rights of citizens, while their duties are left to be taught by families and schools.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: Only statement 1 is from the chapter. Statement 2 is false: the values and ideals usually form the basis for the laws and principles in a constitution. Statement 3 is false: the Constitution lays out the rights and the duties of citizens, and Fundamental Duties are part of it.
o: 1 only
2 and 3 only
1 and 2 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q:
The Kolhapur District Sports Association is drafting a Charter.
Clause 1: A Selection Panel picks teams, a Games Committee runs tournaments and a Grievance Tribunal decides complaints.
Clause 2: The Tribunal may call for the Games Committee's file and ask it to explain any decision.
Clause 3: Every registered player may enter district meets; every player must report an injury within a day.
Clause 4: By 2035 there will be a coaching academy in each taluka.
Member X wants to drop Clause 2 'to save time'. Member Y wants to drop Clause 4 because 'goals are not rules'. Only one clause can be dropped.
(a) Name the part of a constitution that each of Clauses 1, 2 and 4 matches.
(b) Clause 3 holds two kinds of provisions. Name them.
(c) Whose proposal should the meeting accept? Decide and justify with the chapter.
questions.a: (a) Clause 1 is the framework of the organs and their roles; Clause 2 is checks and balances; Clause 4 is a long-term goal. (b) Rights (to enter meets) and duties (to report an injury). (c) Either choice is credited if reasoned. A strong answer drops Clause 4, because checks and balances ensure fairness, responsibility and accountability and are what stop one body from acting unchecked, while a goal can be restated later; but it admits that the chapter counts long-term goals as part of what a constitution lays out, so dropping it is also a loss. The same weight can be given to keeping goals if the answer explains why Clause 2's work can be done in other ways.
s: Part (a): organs, checks and balances, long-term goals matched
Part (b): rights and duties
Part (c): a decision weighed on checks and balances versus goals

questions.q:
At a district kho-kho final in Hyderabad the scores were level. A chaser claimed she had tagged a runner before the runner crossed the line; the runner's team disagreed. The referee opened the official rulebook, and both captains read the page together and agreed on the result. The sports officer now wants one plan to prevent such quarrels. Plan P: both captains sign, before the first whistle, that they accept the rulebook. Plan Q: each captain gets a short rule card at the toss, and the full rulebook stays with the referee, to be shown only if a dispute arises.
(a) What did the rulebook do for the match?
(b) Which document does the same job for the whole nation, and what do the President, the prime minister, the ministers and the judges do in relation to it?
(c) Which plan is closer to how the nation treats its Constitution? Decide and justify with the chapter.
questions.a: (a) It let a dispute be settled amicably, since the captains and the referee looked at one agreed text. (b) The Constitution; the President takes an oath to preserve, protect and defend it, and the prime minister, ministers and judges promise to follow its provisions. (c) Plan P is closer: officials pledge to uphold the Constitution as a commitment made in advance. A reasoned case for Q is credited if it notes the risk that a captain who only meets the rules during a quarrel may not have agreed to them.
s: Part (a): the rulebook settled the dispute amicably
Part (b): the Constitution; officials' oath or promise
Part (c): a decision linking agreement in advance to the officials' pledge

questions.q: A friend argues, 'A country does not need a written constitution; honest leaders and a fair judge are enough.' Argue against her using four things the chapter says a constitution lays out, and the pledge officials take.
questions.a: A written constitution frames the three organs and their roles, so no leader has to guess his power. It sets checks and balances so that fairness, responsibility and accountability do not depend on one leader's honesty. It lays out the rights and duties of citizens, so people know what they may demand. It outlines long-term goals the nation shares beyond any leader. Officials pledge to uphold it, which makes their honesty accountable to a text everyone has accepted, as the captains accepted the rulebook.
s: Organs and roles written down
Checks and balances instead of reliance on honesty
Rights and duties of citizens
Long-term goals of the nation
Pledge to uphold it, like the agreed rulebook

questions.q: Write a short situation from school life in which a written rulebook settles an argument. Then say which part of a country's constitution your rulebook is most like and why.
questions.a: Any valid situation, e.g. two classes dispute a tie in a quiz and the written quiz rules decide it. The rulebook is like the part of the Constitution that sets rules and checks and balances, since both settle disputes by a text everyone accepted earlier.
s: A believable situation where a written rule settles the argument
Names a matching part of the Constitution (organs, checks and balances, rights and duties or goals)
Reason linking the two

questions.q: A school newsletter asks: 'Why is Republic Day on 26 January and not 26 November?' Write a two-sentence headline-and-explanation for the newsletter that uses both dates and the number of days between them.
questions.a: Any correct piece, e.g. 'Republic Day marks the day the Constitution began to work.' The Constitution was adopted on 26 November 1949 but came into effect 61 days later, on 26 January 1950, and Republic Day marks the later date.
s: Gives both dates correctly
States the 61-day gap
Says Republic Day marks the coming into effect

questions.q: Three school questions are put beside the chapter's list of what India's leaders had to decide: (i) 'Which languages will our assemblies use?' (ii) 'Who may vote in school elections?' (iii) 'How will we settle a quarrel between two clubs?' Which of them matches a question the chapter lists, and which does not appear in the chapter's list?
questions.a: (ii) matches 'Who should have the right to vote?' and (iii) matches 'How should we decide on disputes?'. (i) is not among the questions the chapter lists (type of government, rules and principles, right to vote, deciding disputes).
s: (ii) and (iii) matched with the chapter's questions
(i) identified as not in the chapter's list

questions.q: Using the question 'Who should have the right to vote?' as an example, explain how the size and diversity of India made such questions harder than they would be for a small town.
questions.a: India is a large, culturally diverse and complex country, so people from many regions, communities and walks of life had to agree on one rule about voting, where a small town could settle it by a single meeting.
s: Names India's size, diversity and complexity from the chapter
Applies it to reaching one agreed rule on voting

questions.q: The Assembly's members represented India's diverse regions, professions and social groups. Explain why this mattered for writing the Constitution of a country like India.
questions.a: India is large, culturally diverse and complex, so people from different regions, professions and groups bring their own experience and views; this helps the Constitution answer questions about government, voting and disputes in a way acceptable to many.
s: Links to India's size and diversity
Different views and experience from different groups
Conclusion: a Constitution everyone can accept

questions.q: Dr. Sachidananda Sinha wished the Assembly's proceedings to be marked by 'wisdom, toleration, justice, and fairness to all'. Choose any two of these and say how the Assembly's membership (many regions, professions and social groups) made each one more necessary.
questions.a: Any two with a reason, e.g. toleration, because members from different regions and groups held different views and had to accept those unlike their own; fairness to all, because the Constitution was to serve people of every region and group, not only those represented most strongly.
s: Two qualities chosen from the wish
A reason linking each to the members' diversity

questions.q: 'The Constitution of India was made by the people through their representatives.' Justify this statement using what the chapter says about how the Constituent Assembly was formed.
questions.a: Members of the Constituent Assembly were elected by the legislative assemblies of the provinces, whose members had in turn been elected by the people. The Assembly represented diverse regions, professions and social groups and included 15 women. It developed and wrote the Constitution over almost three years and adopted it on 26 November 1949.
s: People elected the provincial legislative assemblies
Those assemblies elected the Assembly members
Diverse regions, professions and groups (and 15 women)
The Assembly itself developed the Constitution over almost three years
Adoption on 26 November 1949

questions.q: Class 7 students stage a mock Constituent Assembly. Each of the six section councils chooses 5 members, and the council members were themselves elected by the students of the section. Which part of the real process do the section councils copy?
questions.a: The real Assembly's members were elected by the legislative assemblies of the provinces, whose members had in turn been elected by the people. The section councils play the part of the provincial legislative assemblies.
o: The provincial legislative assemblies, which elected the members
The people of India, who voted directly for every member
The Drafting Committee, which selected the members of the Assembly
The Chairman of the Assembly, who nominated each member himself

questions.q: Trace the making of the Constitution from the formation of the Assembly to Republic Day. Give the date of each stage, work out how long the Assembly's work took and how long the Constitution waited before coming into effect, and explain what Republic Day celebrates.
questions.a: The Assembly was formed on 9 December 1946 with members elected by the provincial legislative assemblies. A Drafting Committee prepared the initial text, and the Assembly developed and wrote the Constitution. It was adopted on 26 November 1949, 1,083 days after formation, which is almost three years. It came into effect on 26 January 1950, 61 days after adoption. Republic Day celebrates the coming into effect of the Constitution.
s: Formation date and how the members were chosen
Drafting Committee's initial text and the Assembly's writing
Adoption date and 1,083 days (almost three years)
Effect date and 61 days after adoption
Republic Day celebrates the coming into effect

questions.q:
Match each quantity worked out from the chapter's dates and numbers (Column A) with its value (Column B).
Column A: 1. Days from 9 December 1946 to 26 November 1949  2. Days from 26 November 1949 to 26 January 1950  3. Members lost between 389 and 299  4. Women among the members
Column B: a. 61  b. 1,083  c. 90  d. 15
questions.a: From 9 December 1946 to 26 November 1949 is 1,083 days; from 26 November 1949 to 26 January 1950 is 61 days; 389 - 299 = 90; the women members numbered 15.

questions.q:
Read the statements about the Constituent Assembly.
1. It was formed in 1946 with 299 members, a number later increased to 389 after the Partition of India.
2. Its members were elected by the legislative assemblies of the provinces, whose members had in turn been elected by the people.
3. The Drafting Committee that prepared the initial text was chaired by Dr. B.R. Ambedkar, the first Law and Justice minister of independent India.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: Statements 2 and 3 are from the chapter. Statement 1 swaps the numbers: the Assembly began with 389 members and was later reduced to 299 after the Partition.
o: 2 and 3 only
1 and 3 only
1 and 2 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q: The Partition of India cut the Constituent Assembly from 389 members to 299, a fall of about ___ per cent (to the nearest whole number).

A museum in Delhi shows this panel on the Constituent Assembly: 'The Assembly was formed in December 1946. Its members were chosen by the legislative assemblies of the provinces. The Partition of India changed its size. Fifteen of its members were women, and they came from many regions, professions and social groups. Its work was completed in November 1949.'
(a) Give the full date on which the Assembly was formed and the Assembly's size before and after the Partition.
(b) Which event happened on 26 January 1950, and what is it called today?
(c) A visitor says, 'With only 15 women, the Assembly cannot be called representative of India.' State one point in favour and one against the visitor, then give your judgement.
questions.a: (a) 9 December 1946; 389 members, reduced to 299. (b) The Constitution came into effect; celebrated as Republic Day. (c) In favour: only 15 women among so many members. Against: members came from diverse regions, professions and social groups. A judgement that weighs both is credited; either conclusion is acceptable if supported.
s: Part (a): 9 December 1946; 389 reduced to 299
Part (b): Constitution came into effect; Republic Day
Part (c): one point each side and a reasoned judgement

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Republic Day is celebrated every year on 26 January.
Reason (R): The Constitution was adopted on 26 November 1949.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both statements are true, but adoption on 26 November 1949 is not why 26 January is celebrated; that is the date the Constitution came into effect, so R does not explain A.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: True or False: The Constitution was written by the Drafting Committee alone; the Constituent Assembly only celebrated it afterwards. Give a reason for your verdict.
questions.a: False. The Constitution was developed and written by the Constituent Assembly over almost three years, and the Drafting Committee chaired by Dr. B.R. Ambedkar prepared only the initial text.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: the Assembly developed and wrote it; the Committee prepared the initial text

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The members of the Constituent Assembly were elected directly by all the adult citizens of India.
Reason (R): The Indian Constitution is described as drawn up by the people through their representatives.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: A is false: the members were elected by the legislative assemblies of the provinces, not directly by every adult. R is true as the Preamble note in the chapter puts it.
o: A is false, but R is true.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.

questions.q: Meera says, 'The Constitution was written by the Constituent Assembly in almost three years. The Drafting Committee only prepared the initial text, and the members of the Assembly were chosen by the provincial legislative assemblies.' Check each part against the chapter.
questions.a: Meera is right on all three parts. The Assembly developed and wrote the Constitution over almost three years (1,083 days from 9 December 1946 to 26 November 1949). The Drafting Committee prepared the initial text. The members were elected by the legislative assemblies of the provinces.
s: Verdict: right on the whole claim
Checks the 'almost three years' part with the dates
Checks the Drafting Committee and election parts

questions.q:
Nagpur's Kendriya Vidyalaya plans a Mock Constituent Assembly of 60 students for Republic Day week. Plan A: every student in the school votes directly for all 60 members. Plan B: each of the 12 class councils elects 5 members, and the council members were themselves elected by their classmates. During the week, 6 of the 60 mock members must leave for a sports meet.
(a) Which plan copies the way the real Assembly's members were chosen, and by whom were they elected?
(b) The loss of 6 from 60 is what percentage of the mock Assembly? How does it compare with the percentage of the real Assembly lost at the Partition (389 to 299, to the nearest whole number)?
(c) The principal asks which plan to adopt. Decide and justify using the chapter.
questions.a: (a) Plan B; the real members were elected by the legislative assemblies of the provinces, whose members had been elected by the people. (b) 6/60 = 10 per cent; the real loss was 90/389, about 23 per cent, more than twice as large. (c) Either plan is credited if reasoned. Plan B copies the historical process and still rests on the people's vote; Plan A gives every student a direct say. A strong answer states which aim (copying history or direct voice) is chosen and why.
s: Part (a): Plan B; elected by provincial legislative assemblies
Part (b): 10 per cent against about 23 per cent
Part (c): a decision weighing the real process against direct voting

questions.q: Anita says the Constituent Assembly 'worked for exactly three years'. Her teacher asks her to count from the Assembly's formation on 9 December 1946 to the adoption of the Constitution on 26 November 1949 and compare with three full years (from 9 December 1946 to 9 December 1949, which is 1,096 days). By how many days did the Assembly's work fall short of three full years?
questions.a: From 9 December 1946 to 26 November 1949 is 1,083 days, and three full years is 1,096 days, so the work fell short by 13 days. This is why the chapter says 'almost three years'.

questions.q: A project says: 'The Constituent Assembly worked from 9 December 1946 to 26 January 1950, so its work took more than three years.' What is the fault in this reasoning, according to the chapter?
questions.a: The Assembly's work ended with the adoption of the Constitution on 26 November 1949. 26 January 1950 is the date it came into effect, which is why Republic Day falls then. Counting to 26 January adds 61 days that were not part of the writing.
o: The work ended on adoption (26 November 1949); effect came on 26 January 1950
The Assembly started on 26 January 1950, and the project has swapped the two end dates
The work ended on 9 December 1946, the day the first members were elected
The Constitution came into effect first and was adopted by the Assembly later

questions.q: (a) Write the chain through which the people of India were linked to the members of the Constituent Assembly. (b) How does this differ from every adult citizen voting for each Assembly member?
questions.a: (a) The people elected the members of the provincial legislative assemblies, and these assemblies elected the Constituent Assembly's members. (b) The people did not vote for Assembly members themselves; the provincial legislators did so on their behalf.
s: Part (a): people, then provincial legislative assemblies, then Assembly members
Part (b): the legislators voted, so the people did not choose each member directly

questions.q: Rhea says, 'Every idea in our Constitution came from outside, because the makers studied the constitutions of France, the USA, the UK, Ireland and Australia.' Test her claim against the chapter.
questions.a: No. The makers did study these constitutions, but the chapter names two other influences: the experience and ideals of the Indian freedom movement (equality, justice, freedom, fraternity; leaders in the Assembly) and India's civilisational heritage (acceptance of different views, respect for women, Fundamental Duties). Studying others to see what was useful is not the same as taking every idea from them.
s: Verdict: disagrees, with the word 'every'
Names the freedom struggle and its ideals as an Indian source
Names India's civilisational heritage with an example

questions.q:
A Class 7 debate team in Bhubaneswar has four cards for the motion 'Most ideas in our Constitution came from abroad'.
Card 1: Every adult citizen may vote.
Card 2: Citizens have a duty to protect the natural environment.
Card 3: The government is given goals such as a good standard of living, but a court cannot force it to meet them.
Card 4: Judges decide cases free of pressure from the other organs.
(a) For Cards 1 and 2, name the source the chapter would give.
(b) For Cards 3 and 4, name the country that inspired the idea.
(c) The judges ask the team to take a side on the motion using only these cards. Which side would you argue, and what would you say about the chapter's three sources?
questions.a: (a) Card 1: experience of the freedom struggle; Card 2: India's civilisational heritage (emphasis on duties, Nature as sacred). (b) Card 3: Ireland (Directive Principles); Card 4: the USA (independent judiciary). (c) The cards split two and two, so a team may argue either side; a strong answer notes that the chapter names three sources, so no single source accounts for most ideas, and the makers chose what was useful for India.
s: Part (a): freedom struggle for Card 1; heritage for Card 2
Part (b): Ireland for Card 3; USA for Card 4
Part (c): a side chosen with the two-two split and three sources considered

questions.q: A student's poster on 'liberty, equality, fraternity' says these ideals were formulated in the French Declaration of 1789. By the time the Indian Constitution came into effect in 1950, those ideals had already been in public view for ___ years.

The Sanskrit saying 'ā no bhadrāh kratavo yantu viśhwatah' is quoted in the chapter. (i) Give its meaning. (ii) Name two ideas India took from other countries' constitutions, with the country for each. (iii) Name one feature of the Constitution that comes instead from India's own heritage.
questions.a: (i) 'Let noble thoughts come to me from every side.' (ii) Any two of: liberty, equality and fraternity from France; the Directive Principles from Ireland; an independent judiciary from the USA. (iii) Fundamental Duties (or respect for women, acceptance of different views).
s: Meaning of the saying
Two ideas each with the right country
One Indian-heritage feature

questions.q: (a) Which Preamble value is closest in meaning to the saying 'vasudhaiva kutumbakam' (the world is one family)? (b) Give one example from school life where a student acts on that value.
questions.a: (a) Fraternity, the Preamble value that says all of us should behave as members of the same family. (b) Any valid example, such as a class including a new student in its games and never treating her as inferior.
s: Part (a): fraternity, with the family idea
Part (b): a valid school example of treating no one as inferior

questions.q: A student writes, 'The ideals of liberty, equality and fraternity reached India only through France; the freedom struggle never spoke of them.' Which fact in the chapter most directly contradicts her?
questions.a: The chapter lists equality of all, justice for all, freedom and fraternity among the ideals of the Indian freedom struggle that were enshrined in the Constitution. The other facts are true but do not show the freedom struggle holding these ideals.
o: The freedom struggle's ideals included equality, justice, freedom and fraternity
The French Declaration of 1789 focused on equality, liberty and justice for all
The Directive Principles of State Policy were inspired by the Irish Constitution
An independent judiciary was shaped with the help of the American Constitution

questions.q:
Read the statements about the influences on the Constitution.
1. The experience of the freedom struggle helped answer questions such as how the powers of the executive, the legislature and the judiciary are kept separate.
2. The idea of the Directive Principles of State Policy was taken from the American Constitution.
3. Respect for women and the saying sarve bhavantu sukhinah are among the principles of India's culture that find a place in the Constitution, though expressed a little differently.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: Statements 1 and 3 are from the chapter. Statement 2 is false: the Directive Principles were inspired by the Irish Constitution; the American Constitution helped shape the concept of an independent judiciary.
o: 1 and 3 only
1 only
2 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The makers of the Constitution studied the constitutions of France, USA, UK, Ireland, Australia and other democratic countries.
Reason (R): The Indian tradition says 'Let noble thoughts come to me from every side'.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both statements are true, and the chapter itself gives R as the tradition in whose spirit the makers studied other constitutions, so R explains A.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: A quiz card says: 'The experience of the freedom struggle helped India's leaders answer many 'how' and 'what' questions about the Constitution.' Which of these is one of the questions the chapter lists as answered that way?
questions.a: The chapter lists five such questions: the right of every adult citizen to vote; keeping the powers of the three organs separate; guaranteeing fundamental rights; the process of amending the Constitution; and the relationship between the Central and State governments. The other questions are not in that list.
o: What should be the process if we want to amend the Constitution?
Which country's constitution should inspire the Directive Principles?
Who should chair the committee that prepares the initial text?
Which scenes should illustrate the pages of the Constitution?

questions.q: The answer to a quiz question is 'France, 1789'. Write a question that has this answer and explain in two lines how the answer is linked to the Indian Constitution.
questions.a: Example: 'Where and when did the Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen come from?' The ideals of liberty, equality and fraternity in India's Constitution were adopted from France's constitution, which enshrined them from the French Revolution of 1789.
s: A suitable question with this answer
Names the ideals of liberty, equality and fraternity
Link: adopted from France's constitution into India's

questions.q: Three clauses are proposed: (i) the legislature may not tell a court how to decide a case; (ii) the State shall work to give everyone a good standard of living, though no court can force it; (iii) all citizens enjoy liberty, equality and fraternity. (a) Give for each the country the chapter names as its source. (b) Which clause is a goal and not an enforceable right?
questions.a: (a) (i) the USA (an independent judiciary); (ii) Ireland (Directive Principles); (iii) France (liberty, equality, fraternity). (b) Clause (ii) is a goal, because a Directive Principle cannot be taken to a judge.
s: Part (a): all three sources matched correctly
Part (b): clause (ii) identified as a goal not enforceable in court

questions.q: 'The makers of the Constitution were open to learning from the world but did not give up their own roots.' Justify this using the chapter.
questions.a: They followed the tradition of 'let noble thoughts come to me from every side' and studied the constitutions of France, USA, UK, Ireland and Australia, taking liberty, equality and fraternity, Directive Principles and an independent judiciary. Yet the freedom struggle and India's heritage (Fundamental Duties, respect for women, unity of India) remained the base.
s: States the tradition of openness to ideas from every side
Names the countries studied
Two ideas that came from abroad
Two ideas that came from India's own experience and heritage

questions.q: The chapter says the makers studied the constitutions of France, the USA, the UK, Ireland, Australia and other countries. (a) For which of these five countries does the chapter name a specific idea that India took? (b) What reason does it give for studying all of them?
questions.a: (a) France (liberty, equality, fraternity), Ireland (Directive Principles) and the USA (independent judiciary); no specific idea is named from the UK or Australia. (b) To explore their usefulness for India's context, in the Indian spirit of 'let noble thoughts come to me from every side'.
s: Part (a): France, Ireland and the USA; none named for UK or Australia
Part (b): to explore usefulness for India's context

questions.q: True or False: The Fundamental Duties must have been borrowed from another country's constitution, since duties of citizens are not found in India's own traditions. Give a reason for your verdict.
questions.a: False. The chapter says India's heritage and history show a great emphasis on the duties and role of the people in governance, so it was natural for the makers to incorporate Fundamental Duties from our own civilisational heritage.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: duties come from India's own emphasis on the duties and role of the people

questions.q:
Assertion (A): India's Constitution adopted the ideals of liberty, equality and fraternity from the French constitution.
Reason (R): Equality of all, justice for all, freedom and fraternity were also ideals of the Indian freedom struggle.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both statements are true, but the Indian freedom struggle's ideals do not explain why the French constitution is the source of these ideals; they are a second influence, so R does not explain A.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: Two students argue whether the ideal of fraternity came into the Constitution from the freedom struggle or from the French constitution. (a) Using the chapter, explain why both can be right. (b) Name one other ideal that appears both in the freedom struggle's list of ideals and in the French trio.
questions.a: (a) The chapter lists fraternity among the ideals of the Indian freedom struggle and also says 'liberty, equality, fraternity' were adopted from the French constitution, so one ideal can have more than one source. (b) Equality (freedom/liberty is also accepted).
s: Part (a): fraternity named in both the freedom struggle list and the French trio
Part (b): equality, or freedom/liberty

questions.q: A village panchayat's charter has two clauses. Clause X lists goals such as clean drinking water for every family, which no villager can force the panchayat to meet through a judge. Clause Y says the committee that hears complaints must decide free of pressure from the sarpanch. Which pair of sources does the chapter give for the ideas behind X and Y?
questions.a: Goals that a court cannot enforce are Directive Principles, an idea inspired by the Irish Constitution; a judiciary free from the other organs is the concept the American Constitution helped shape.
o: X from the Irish Constitution, Y from the American Constitution
X from the American Constitution, Y from the Irish Constitution
X from the French Constitution, Y from the Irish Constitution
X from the Irish Constitution, Y from the French Constitution

questions.q: Compare the Indian freedom movement and other countries' constitutions as influences on the Constitution. Say what kind of thing each supplied, with examples, and explain why the makers needed both.
questions.a: The freedom movement supplied ideals and experience: equality of all, justice for all, freedom, fraternity, the idea of the Constitution as a tool for achieving them, and leaders who sat in the Assembly and answered 'how' questions (every adult's vote, separation of powers, fundamental rights, amending the Constitution, Centre-State relations). Other constitutions supplied working models: liberty, equality and fraternity from France, Directive Principles from Ireland, an independent judiciary from the USA. Ideals alone do not say how government should be arranged, and models alone do not say what a nation stands for, so the makers used both.
s: Freedom movement: ideals and experience with two examples
Other constitutions: models with two examples
Why both were needed

questions.q: Four students each pair an idea of the Constitution with its source. Neel: the way every adult citizen gets the vote, from the experience of the freedom struggle. Pia: Fundamental Duties, from the Irish Constitution. Sam: respect for women, from India's civilisational heritage. Tina: an independent judiciary, from the American Constitution. Whose pairing does NOT agree with the chapter?
questions.a: Fundamental Duties come from India's civilisational heritage, which put great emphasis on the duties and role of the people in governance. The Irish Constitution inspired the Directive Principles. The other three pairings are as the chapter gives them.
o: Pia
Neel
Sam
Tina

questions.q:
Arjun in Kochi is having tea with his grandfather, who says, 'In our village the elders always heard people who thought differently, and every villager knew the duties he owed to the village.' Arjun later reads that Begum Aizaz Rasul told the Constituent Assembly on 22 November 1949 that women's equality was 'no new concept' but an ideal long cherished by India. Arjun can add only one example to the school exhibit on India's heritage: Fundamental Duties, or respect for women.
(a) Which two ideas from the chapter's discussion of India's heritage did the grandfather's words show?
(b) Which feature of the Constitution reflects the emphasis on duties?
(c) Which one example should Arjun choose for the exhibit? Give two chapter-based reasons.
questions.a: (a) Acceptance that people can have different points of view; the emphasis on duties and the role of the people in governance. (b) Fundamental Duties. (c) Either choice is acceptable if supported: Fundamental Duties are directly traced to the heritage of duties in governance; respect for women is a heritage principle and Begum Aizaz Rasul called women's equality an ideal long cherished by India.
s: Part (a): different points of view; duties
Part (b): Fundamental Duties
Part (c): one example chosen with two reasons from the chapter

questions.q: Rohan says, 'Article 48-A makes the government responsible for protecting the environment, so a Class 7 student has no duty about it.' Mina says, 'The Constitution also asks every citizen to protect the natural environment.' Who is right according to the chapter?
questions.a: Article 48-A on environment and wildlife protection is a Directive Principle that guides the government, and one of the Fundamental Duties is to protect and improve the natural environment, including forests, lakes, rivers and wildlife. Citizens have a duty even though the government has a goal.
o: Mina: Article 48-A guides the government, and a duty also asks every citizen to protect it
Rohan: Article 48-A is a Fundamental Right, so a court takes over the duty of protecting the environment
Mina: Article 48-A is a Fundamental Duty, so the government itself has no responsibility for it
Rohan: Directive Principles bind only the citizens, and the government is free to leave them out

questions.q:
A Gram Sabha in a Bihar village received four letters.
Letter 1: A man says he sees no reason to respect the national flag and the national anthem.
Letter 2: Many families say they do not get enough nutrition and ask the government to improve it.
Letter 3: A landlord refused to rent a room to a family because of their caste.
Letter 4: The village school refused admission to a nine-year-old girl, saying it keeps places for boys.
The Gram Sabha has funds to support only one court case this year.
(a) Label each letter as a Fundamental Right, a Fundamental Duty or a Directive Principle.
(b) For which letters can the chapter say a judge will help, and why not for the others?
(c) Letters 3 and 4 are both court-worthy. Which one should the Gram Sabha take up this year? Decide, justify, and say what villagers can still do about Letter 2.
questions.a: (a) Letter 1: Fundamental Duty (respecting the national flag and anthem); Letter 2: Directive Principle (Article 47); Letter 3: Fundamental Right to equality; Letter 4: Fundamental Right (Article 21-A, right to education, and equality). (b) Letters 3 and 4: Fundamental Rights are promises that can be demanded in court when someone is treated unfairly because of who she is. Letter 2 is a goal for the government that a judge cannot be asked to enforce; Letter 1 is a duty the chapter asks citizens to follow. (c) Either is credited if reasoned, e.g. Letter 4 because it affects a child's schooling now and the right to education is a stated Article (21-A), or Letter 3 because it is a clear case of unfair treatment because of who the family is. For Letter 2 villagers can press the government to make efforts, but cannot ask a judge to force it.
s: Part (a): all four letters labelled correctly
Part (b): Letters 3 and 4 enforceable; Letters 1 and 2 not, with reasons
Part (c): a reasoned choice between Letters 3 and 4, and what villagers can still do about Letter 2

questions.q: Mayor Kavita proposes that the legislature itself should decide whether its own laws follow the Constitution. Show, using the chapter's idea of organs of government, why this arrangement cannot work well.
questions.a: The chapter gives this job to the judiciary, which ensures that laws made are in accordance with the Constitution. The legislature makes laws, and separation of powers is essential to effective working; if one organ made and checked its own laws, checks and balances would be lost.
s: States that the judiciary ensures laws accord with the Constitution
States that the legislature makes laws and powers must be separate
Concludes that checking its own laws removes the check

questions.q: Anil's village has many undernourished children. He says, 'Article 47 speaks of nutrition and public health, so I will go to court and make the government feed them today.' Which reply fits the chapter?
questions.a: Article 47 is a Directive Principle. If the government does not make efforts, one cannot go to a judge to complain. Fundamental Rights, in contrast, are enforceable.
o: He cannot; Directive Principles are goals, not enforceable in court
He can, because Article 47 is a Fundamental Right just like Article 14 is
He can, but only after the panchayat first passes its own law on nutrition
He cannot, because the Constitution does not mention nutrition anywhere

questions.q: Parliament passes a law banning single-use plastic bags. The district collector's office enforces it. A shopkeeper goes to the High Court and says one clause goes against the Constitution. Describe what each organ of government does in this story, explain what 'separation of powers' protects, and say which feature of the Constitution the shopkeeper's challenge shows.
questions.a: Parliament, the legislature, makes the law. The district collector's office is part of the executive, which implements the law and is headed by the prime minister. The court, the judiciary, ensures that laws made are in accordance with the Constitution and decides whether a law has been broken. Separation of powers is essential to their effective working, since no one organ both makes and judges its own acts. The challenge shows checks and balances, which ensure fairness, responsibility and accountability.
s: Legislature makes the law
Executive implements it
Judiciary tests it against the Constitution
Separation of powers explained
Checks and balances named for the challenge

questions.q: Neha says, 'The legislature makes the laws and the executive, headed by the prime minister, carries them out, so the judiciary only decides punishments for people who break the law.' How far is she right?
questions.a: Partly right. The legislature does make the laws and the executive, headed by the prime minister, implements them, and the judiciary does decide whether a law has been broken and the punishment. But 'only' is wrong: the judiciary also ensures that all laws made are in accordance with the Constitution.
s: Verdict: partly right
The right part: legislature makes, executive implements, judiciary decides breaches
The wrong part: the judiciary also checks laws against the Constitution

questions.q: Compare Fundamental Rights, Fundamental Duties and Directive Principles of State Policy. For each, say whom it addresses and whether a judge can enforce it, and give one example from the chapter's infographic.
questions.a: Fundamental Rights (e.g. Right to Equality, Article 14) are promises to citizens that must be kept: a judge can help someone treated unfairly because of who she is. Fundamental Duties (e.g. to protect and improve the natural environment) are what citizens are expected to follow. Directive Principles (e.g. Article 47 on nutrition) are goals that the government should try to achieve; a judge cannot be asked to enforce them, and they are more like guidelines. The makers wanted some rights to be demanded at once and some bigger goals that might take time.
s: Fundamental Rights: addressee, enforceability, example
Fundamental Duties: addressee and example
Directive Principles: addressee, not enforceable, example

questions.q: Rohan says, 'Article 44 (Uniform Civil Code) carries an Article number in the chapter's infographic, so it is a Fundamental Right I can enforce in court.' What is the best correction?
questions.a: A number does not make a provision a right. The infographic lists Article 44 among the Directive Principles of State Policy, which are goals for the government and cannot be taken to a judge, while the Right against Exploitation is a Fundamental Right even though no number is shown for it.
o: Article 44 is a Directive Principle, a goal for the government that a judge cannot be asked to enforce
Article 44 is a Fundamental Duty, so every citizen must obey it and the court will punish those who do not
Article 44 is a Fundamental Right for citizens who ask the government first, and only then can a judge enforce it
Article 44 is a Fundamental Right, but the infographic shows only the Directive Principles with Article numbers

questions.q: Under the Fundamental Duty about a child's education, a parent must give opportunities from the lower to the upper age limit named in the chapter. Mr. Das enrols his daughter on the day she reaches the lower limit. The duty then covers her for ___ more years.

Assertion (A): Article 21-A makes education a Fundamental Right.
Reason (R): A Fundamental Duty asks a parent or guardian to provide opportunities for education to a child between the age of six and fourteen years.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both statements are true, but the duty of the parent is a separate provision; it is not the reason why education is a Fundamental Right, so R does not explain A.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: Choose any three Fundamental Duties from the chapter and give one way in which a Class 7 student can follow each.
questions.a: For example: respect the National Flag and National Anthem by standing in attention during assembly; protect the environment by not littering and planting saplings; value heritage by visiting a local monument carefully; strive for excellence in studies and sports.
s: First duty with a realistic way to follow it
Second duty with a way
Third duty with a way

questions.q: True or False: A family refused a rented room because of their caste may ask a court for help, but a group of villagers cannot ask a court to force the government to improve nutrition under Article 47; the makers designed the Constitution with both kinds of provisions on purpose. Give a reason for your verdict.
questions.a: True. Fundamental Rights are promises that must be kept, so a judge can help someone treated unfairly because of who she is; Directive Principles are goals, not rules a judge can enforce. The makers wanted some rights demanded immediately and some bigger goals that might take time as the country progressed.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: rights are enforceable, DPSP are goals, both created on purpose

questions.q:
Read the statements about the Constitution's key features.
1. A person refused service by a shopkeeper because of who she is can go to court, since Fundamental Rights are promises that must be kept.
2. Article 38 (social, political and economic justice) and Article 47 (nutrition, standard of living and public health) are both among the Directive Principles in the chapter's infographic.
3. The Fundamental Duty about education speaks to a parent or guardian whose child is between six and fourteen years of age.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: All three agree with the chapter: Fundamental Rights can be demanded in court, Articles 38 and 47 are Directive Principles in the infographic, and the education duty is addressed to a parent or guardian of a child between six and fourteen.
o: 1, 2 and 3
1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
1 and 3 only

questions.q: The makers wanted some rights that could be demanded at once and some bigger goals that might take time. (a) Which of these is the group of Fundamental Rights and which the Directive Principles? (b) Using Article 38 (social, political and economic justice), explain why a goal of that kind is placed among those that take time.
questions.a: (a) Fundamental Rights can be demanded immediately; Directive Principles are the bigger goals. (b) Social, political and economic justice for all is a large aim that a country reaches step by step as it progresses, so it cannot be promised as a right to be enforced today.
s: Part (a): rights at once, Directive Principles as bigger goals
Part (b): a large aim needing time as the country progresses

questions.q: A town council wants to protect an old fort and the wetland next to it. (a) Which two Articles in the chapter's list of Directive Principles support this? (b) If the council does nothing, why can a citizen not ask a judge to force it?
questions.a: (a) Article 49 (protection of monuments, places and objects of national importance) and Article 48-A (environment and wildlife protection). (b) Directive Principles are goals and guidelines for the government, not promises that a judge can enforce.
s: Part (a): Articles 49 and 48-A
Part (b): Directive Principles are goals, not enforceable in court

questions.q:
A Class 7 class in Mysuru makes one quiz card for each item in the chapter's infographic: six Fundamental Duties (a to f), four Fundamental Rights (Equality, Article 14; Freedom, Article 21; Right against Exploitation; Education, Article 21-A) and six Directive Principles (Articles 38, 41, 44, 47, 48-A, 49). The quiz is too long, and the class must drop exactly six cards: either the six Duty cards or the six Directive Principle cards.
(a) How many cards are for provisions a judge can enforce, and how many are for goals she cannot be asked to enforce?
(b) The Duty cards speak to whom, and the Directive Principle cards speak to whom?
(c) Which set of six should be dropped? Decide and justify with the chapter.
questions.a: (a) 4 cards for Fundamental Rights, which a judge can enforce; 6 cards for Directive Principles, which she cannot. (b) The Duty cards speak to citizens; the Directive Principle cards speak to the government. (c) Either choice is credited if reasoned. Dropping the Directive Principles loses the picture of the social and economic vision the makers had for India, but they are guidelines and not enforceable; dropping the Duties loses what students themselves are expected to do now, such as protecting rivers, and the Duties are the part the class can act on. A strong answer names what is lost with its choice.
s: Part (a): 4 enforceable rights and 6 goals
Part (b): duties address citizens, Directive Principles address the government
Part (c): a decision that weighs the vision of Directive Principles against what citizens can do

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A citizen cannot go to a judge when the government fails to follow a Directive Principle.
Reason (R): The makers expected every goal in the Directive Principles to be achieved on the day the Constitution came into effect.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: A is true. R is false: the makers wanted some bigger goals that might take time to achieve as the country progressed.
o: A is true, but R is false.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q:
Match each situation (Column A) with the part of the Constitution it belongs to (Column B).
Column A: 1. A resident clears litter from the river bank near her house.  2. A court tells a guest house it cannot turn a family away because of their caste.  3. The government opens a nutrition programme in line with Article 47.  4. A girl of nine is admitted to school under Article 21-A.
Column B: a. Fundamental Duty  b. Directive Principle  c. Fundamental Right to equality  d. Fundamental Right to education
questions.a: Clearing litter is the duty to protect the natural environment; the court acts on the Right to Equality; Article 47 is a Directive Principle; Article 21-A is the right to education.

questions.q: Distinguish between a Fundamental Duty and a Directive Principle on two points: who is expected to act, and one example of each from the chapter's infographic.
questions.a: A Fundamental Duty is something citizens are expected to follow, e.g. to protect and improve the natural environment. A Directive Principle is a goal the government should try to achieve, e.g. Article 47 on nutrition, standard of living and public health.
s: Fundamental Duty: addressed to citizens, with an example
Directive Principle: a goal for the government, with an example

questions.q: In a village, 150 eligible citizens living in a distant hamlet are left out of the voters' list. (a) Which line of the chapter's account of the electoral system does this go against? (b) To which tier of government and which system does the Gram Panchayat belong?
questions.a: (a) The Constitution has laid down an electoral system to ensure that every eligible citizen is enabled to vote. (b) The local tier, the Panchayati Raj system.
s: Part (a): every eligible citizen must be enabled to vote
Part (b): the local tier, Panchayati Raj

questions.q: The Panchayati Raj system was integrated into the Constitution in 1992, which is ___ years after Part IV-A was added in 1976.

The chapter says the government also creates opportunities for people to give feedback on proposed laws or changes in rules. (a) Give one benefit of seeking such feedback before a rule is finalised. (b) Name one other way, listed in the chapter, in which a group of citizens can influence change.
questions.a: (a) The people who will live with the rule can point out problems and show whether it is fair and workable. (b) Popular movements can initiate changes.
s: Part (a): a valid benefit of feedback
Part (b): popular movements, or a citizen's challenge in court

questions.q: Hina says, 'Duties of citizens are an old Indian idea, so Part IV-A on Fundamental Duties must have been in the Constitution from the start.' Which reply agrees with the chapter?
questions.a: The chapter links Fundamental Duties to India's heritage of emphasis on duties, but says Part IV-A was added in 1976, so the idea is old while the Part was added later through an amendment.
o: The idea is old, but Part IV-A was added to the Constitution only in 1976
The idea is from France, and Part IV-A was added in 1950 along with the Preamble
Part IV-A came into effect on 26 January 1950, and the 1976 change only renamed it
Part IV-A was added by the Supreme Court's 2004 flag ruling

questions.q:
The civics club of a Jaipur school plans a wall display with the heading 'How our Constitution changes'. Sunita's notes say: '2004: a citizen challenged a rule about homes. 1992: the 73rd Amendment. 1976: a new Part was added; three words were also put in the Preamble.' The display has space for only two entries and the club wants the two to show different routes of change.
(a) Which Part was added in 1976, and what is it about?
(b) What did the 73rd Amendment bring into the Constitution?
(c) Which two entries should the club choose to show different routes of change? Justify your choice.
questions.a: (a) Part IV-A, Fundamental Duties. (b) The Panchayati Raj system. (c) One entry from the amendments (1976 or 1992) and the 2004 court ruling, since one is a change by Parliament's amendment and the other a change through a citizen's challenge decided by the Supreme Court. Any reasoned pair showing two routes is credited.
s: Part (a): Part IV-A, Fundamental Duties
Part (b): Panchayati Raj system
Part (c): two entries from different routes with reason

questions.q: Naina's grandfather says, 'Our Panchayati Raj came with the Constitution in 1950.' Her teacher corrects him using the chapter's dates, and Naina works out the gap from 1950. Which correction is right?
questions.a: The chapter says Panchayati Raj was not part of the original Constitution; it was integrated in 1992 with the 73rd Constitutional Amendment Act, which is 1992 - 1950 = 42 years after the Constitution came into effect.
o: Integrated in 1992 through the 73rd Amendment, 42 years after it came into effect
Integrated in 1976 through the 42nd Amendment, 26 years after it came into effect
Integrated in 1992 through the 73rd Amendment, 16 years after it came into effect
Integrated in 2004 by a Supreme Court ruling, 54 years after it came into effect

questions.q: Zoya says, 'Every change to the Constitution since 1950 was started by Parliament, so ordinary citizens can only watch.' Test her claim with the chapter.
questions.a: No. The chapter says some changes can be initiated by popular movements, and opinions are sought from the general public before changes are accepted. Parliament debates amendments, but it is not the only starting point, and citizens are not mere spectators.
s: Verdict: disagrees
Popular movements can initiate changes
Opinions of the general public are sought

questions.q: The Constitution's pages carry scenes from Mohenjo-daro to the freedom movement, such as a gurukula, a scene from the Mahabharata, Nataraja and Nalanda. (a) What do such scenes suggest about what the makers wanted the book to be rooted in? (b) Which of the chapter's three influences on the Constitution does this choice of scenes match most closely?
questions.a: (a) The long history and culture of India, which the makers wanted to carry into the Constitution. (b) India's civilisational heritage.
s: Part (a): rooted in India's long history and culture
Part (b): civilisational heritage

questions.q: A debater says, 'The Constitution is more than a legal document.' Which fact from the chapter best supports this?
questions.a: The chapter says the Constitution is not just a legal document but also a work of art: its text was written by hand by a calligrapher and its pages were illustrated with scenes from Indian history. The other facts describe its legal, rulebook role.
o: Its text was hand-written and its pages carry scenes from Indian history
It sets out checks and balances among the legislature, executive and judiciary
Officials such as the President, ministers and judges pledge to uphold it
It now has 25 parts and 12 schedules

questions.q: After the 2004 flag ruling the chapter adds that the tricolour should 'never be dishonoured'. (a) Which Fundamental Duty in the chapter's list does this reminder connect to? (b) Explain how a right and a duty sit together in this example.
questions.a: (a) The duty to abide by the Constitution and respect its ideals and institutions, the National Flag and the National Anthem. (b) The right to freedom of expression lets citizens fly the flag; the duty requires that they respect it and never dishonour it.
s: Part (a): duty to respect the National Flag
Part (b): right to fly it with the duty not to dishonour it

questions.q: A citizens' group, Nagar Manch, asks who gets a say when a change to the Constitution is proposed. Which description fits the chapter?
questions.a: The chapter says amendments are rigorously debated in Parliament, some also need a debate in the legislative assemblies, and many times opinions are sought from the general public. The wrong options give the job to a court alone, to one person, or to a body that no longer meets.
o: Parliament debates it; some changes also go to legislative assemblies; the public's opinion may also be sought
Parliament votes quickly; the Supreme Court alone decides whether it is needed; the public is never consulted
The President alone decides after hearing the Prime Minister, and no assembly debates the change
The Constituent Assembly meets again for each change and all its original members vote on it

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The Constitution cannot be changed once it has been adopted.
Reason (R): Some changes to the Constitution can be initiated by popular movements.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: A is false: the Constitution can be amended, and the chapter calls it a living document. R is true, and it in fact contradicts A.
o: A is false, but R is true.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.

questions.q:
Read the statements about how the Constitution changes.
1. Part IV-A on Fundamental Duties was added to the Constitution in 1976, after it came into effect.
2. Opinions of the general public are sought on some changes, and some changes need a debate in the legislative assemblies as well as in Parliament.
3. The Panchayati Raj system was in the original Constitution of 1950 and was only renamed by the 73rd Amendment in 1992.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: Statements 1 and 2 are from the chapter. Statement 3 is false: Panchayati Raj was not part of the original Constitution and was integrated in it in 1992.
o: 1 and 2 only
1 only
2 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q: True or False: Because the Constitution is a living document that can be amended, any change to it can be made easily and without much debate. Give a reason for your verdict.
questions.a: False. The chapter says changes (amendments) are rigorously debated in Parliament before they are accepted, some require debate in legislative assemblies as well, and many times opinions are sought from the general public. Being able to change does not mean it changes casually.
s: Verdict: False
Reason: amendments are rigorously debated; others are consulted

questions.q: The chapter calls the Constitution both 'a living document' and 'a work of art'. State one fact from the chapter that supports each description.
questions.a: Living document: it can be changed by amendments, e.g. Part IV-A was added in 1976 and Panchayati Raj in 1992. Work of art: its text was written by hand by Prem Behari Narain Raizada and illustrated by Nandalal Bose and his team.
s: A fact showing it can change
A fact showing it is a work of art

questions.q: Examine the three changes the chapter describes: Part IV-A (1976), the integration of Panchayati Raj by the 73rd Amendment (1992) and the Supreme Court's flag ruling (2004). For each, say what changed, how it came about and what it shows about the Constitution, and then explain why the chapter says every amendment is debated rigorously.
questions.a: Part IV-A: Fundamental Duties were added by an amendment, showing that new parts can be added. Panchayati Raj: not in the original Constitution, it was integrated in 1992 by the 73rd Amendment, showing the Constitution can add structures the country needs. Flag ruling: a citizen challenged a rule in court and the Supreme Court agreed that flying the flag is part of freedom of expression, showing that citizens can start change. Amendments are debated rigorously because they alter the document everyone's rights and duties rest on.
s: Part IV-A with route and lesson
Panchayati Raj with route and lesson
Flag ruling with route and lesson
Reason for rigorous debate

questions.q: A Class 7 council wants to change one rule in its own class constitution. Borrowing from how the chapter says the national Constitution is changed, write a three-step procedure for the council and say which of the chapter's features each step copies.
questions.a: Any workable procedure, e.g. (1) the proposed change is debated rigorously by the council, copying the debate in Parliament; (2) it is also debated by the section representatives, copying the legislative assemblies; (3) classmates' opinions are sought before it is accepted, copying the public feedback.
s: A three-step procedure that could work
Steps linked to debate by the main body and the wider assemblies
A step that seeks the opinion of those affected

questions.q: 'A good constitution should be easy to change.' Evaluate this statement using the chapter's account of how the Indian Constitution is changed and why the makers allowed change.
questions.a: For: the makers realised a need for new laws and rules would emerge, so Part IV-A (1976) and Panchayati Raj (1992) could be added and the Constitution is a living document that can be improved as needs change. Against: every change is rigorously debated in Parliament, some need debate in the legislative assemblies too, and the public is consulted, so change is deliberately careful. Judgement: the chapter supports a Constitution that can change, but not one that changes easily; a good balance is change after wide debate.
s: Reason for allowing change with two examples
Safeguards: debate, assemblies, public opinion
A balanced judgement

questions.q: Arrange these in the order they took place and say what each shows: (i) the Supreme Court's flag ruling, (ii) the 73rd Amendment on Panchayati Raj, (iii) the addition of Part IV-A. How many years separate the earliest and the latest of the three?
questions.a: Order: Part IV-A (1976), Panchayati Raj (1992), flag ruling (2004). Part IV-A and Panchayati Raj are additions by amendment; the flag ruling shows a court interpreting a right. 2004 - 1976 = 28 years.
s: Correct order with years
What each shows (amendments and court interpretation)
28 years

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Part IV-A on Fundamental Duties could be added to the Constitution in 1976, long after 1950.
Reason (R): The makers realised that a need for new laws and rules would emerge over time.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both statements are true, and R explains A: because the makers expected new needs, the Constitution allows amendments, and Part IV-A was added by one.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q:
The Anand Nagar Library Society (240 members) wants to change one rule in its own constitution. Plan 1: the five-member committee votes on the change next Sunday. Plan 2: the committee drafts it and puts it on the notice board for two weeks for comments, the whole general body debates and votes, and if 40 members sign a petition the committee must also put a proposal of the signatories to the general body. Plan 2 would take a month longer.
(a) Which two features of the Constitution's way of changing do the notice-board comments and the general body's debate copy?
(b) Which feature of Plan 2 is the library's version of a 'popular movement'?
(c) Which plan should be used for a change that raises every member's fee, and would your answer differ for a change in closing time by fifteen minutes? Decide and justify.
questions.a: (a) Public feedback on proposed changes (opinions sought from the general public) and debate in a wider body, like the legislative assemblies after Parliament. (b) The petition signed by 40 members. (c) Either position is credited if reasoned. For a fee change affecting everyone, Plan 2: the chapter stresses rigorous debate and public opinion, and the extra month buys fairness. For a fifteen-minute change, Plan 1 may be acceptable since the stakes are low and speed has value, though the same reasoning could be used to defend Plan 2 for both.
s: Part (a): public feedback and debate in a wider body
Part (b): the petition by members
Part (c): a decision that weighs speed against wide debate for different stakes

questions.q: A student may think what she likes about a school rule but is stopped from writing about it in the school magazine. (a) Which of the three areas listed under Liberty (what citizens think, how they express it, how they act on it) is being restricted? (b) Does the Preamble's wording say that no restriction at all can ever be placed on expression? Explain.
questions.a: (a) How she wishes to express her thoughts. (b) No: the chapter says there are no unreasonable restrictions, so it rules out unreasonable restrictions, not every restriction.
s: Part (a): the area of expressing thoughts
Part (b): only unreasonable restrictions are ruled out

questions.q: The chapter says the core values are present across the Constitution, but their essence is written in the Preamble. (a) Article 14 (equality before law) in the infographic matches which Preamble value? (b) Article 38 (social, political and economic justice) matches which?
questions.a: (a) Equality, which the Preamble explains as all being equal before the law. (b) Justice, the value that rules out discrimination and asks the government to work for welfare.
s: Part (a): Equality
Part (b): Justice

questions.q: True or False: A country whose head of state is elected by the people can still be a Republic in the Preamble's sense even if the person elected happens to be the child of the previous head of state. Give a reason for your verdict.
questions.a: True. The chapter explains a Republic as one in which the head of state is an elected person and not a hereditary position. What matters is that the post is filled by election and not by birth, so the family of the person elected does not by itself decide the matter.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: the test is election, not birth into the post

questions.q: Distinguish between Equality and Fraternity as the chapter explains them: which one is about being treated alike by the law and the government, and which is about how citizens behave towards one another? Give the chapter's wording for each.
questions.a: Equality: all are equal before the law and the government should ensure equal opportunity for all. Fraternity: all of us should behave as if we are members of the same family and no one should treat a fellow citizen as inferior.
s: Equality: before the law and equal opportunity
Fraternity: behaviour like one family, no one inferior

questions.q:
A district in Assam announces two steps: (1) a limit on how much farmland a single big estate can own; (2) scholarships for children from the less advantaged families of the district. A critic says, 'Scholarships treat students unequally because only some get them.'
(a) Which Preamble value does step (1) show and what does the chapter say the government may regulate?
(b) Using the chapter's phrase 'welfare of ... less advantaged groups', name the value step (2) shows. Was the value in step (1) part of the original Preamble or added in 1976?
(c) Does the critic have a point? Decide with the chapter's meanings of Equality and Justice.
questions.a: (a) Socialist; the ownership of land and industry. (b) Justice (welfare of less advantaged groups); Socialist was added in 1976 by the 42nd Amendment. (c) Either view if justified: Equality asks for equal opportunity and Justice asks for welfare especially of less advantaged groups, so scholarships can create equal opportunity; a critic's point about fairness to others may be noted.
s: Part (a): Socialist; regulating ownership of land and industry
Part (b): Justice; Socialist added in 1976
Part (c): a reasoned decision using Equality and Justice

questions.q: A poster lists nine value words of the Preamble: sovereign, socialist, secular, democratic, republic, justice, liberty, equality, fraternity. Going by the chapter's note on the 42nd Amendment, the number of these nine that were already in the Preamble before 1976 is ___.

Assertion (A): A scholarship scheme for children from less advantaged families can be defended as consistent with the Preamble's Justice.
Reason (R): The chapter explains Justice as including the government working for the welfare of all, especially of less advantaged groups.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both statements are true, and R explains A: the scheme is a way of working for the welfare of less advantaged groups, which the chapter includes in Justice.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: A small country's rulers are elected, and its constitution was drawn up by the people's representatives. But an ambassador of a neighbouring power must approve every major law before it comes into force. Which of the Preamble words, as the chapter explains them, does this country fail to meet?
